subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage:
Thursday. The checkout page on the site Gurleen looked after went down at ten past four, and five people crowded behind her chair. Her heart hammered. She changed three settings at once, then a fourth, and the page still failed. Harsha, the team lead, said quietly, "What changed last?" She stopped typing.
Friday. She wrote a card, "What changed last? One change. Note it. Check." and taped it to her monitor.
The next Wednesday a smaller alert fired. Gurleen breathed out, rolled back the last update, watched the page come back and wrote down the time.

qa.q: When did the checkout page go down?
qa.a: The checkout page went down at ten past four on Thursday.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling as she changed the settings with five people behind her?
qa.a: Gurleen felt panicky, with her heart hammering and thinking narrowed, so she changed several settings at once.

qa.q: What turning point helped Gurleen on the next Wednesday?
qa.a: She had written a card reminding her of one change at a time, and she used it to roll back the last update and note the time.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Gurleen's changing of many settings at once?
qa.a: Harsha sees the pressure and asks a quiet question, "What changed last?", to slow things down.

grounding: Shows a young engineer feeling rising panic in a live failure, changing many things, then adopting a one-change routine.

subtopic: Debugging and problem solving under pressure
passage: I am Minakshi, and my first live failure taught me more than any course. The report job emailed itself twice to every customer, and my whole team stood behind my chair. My hands were cold and my head felt narrow as a tube. In one minute I changed the schedule, then the file path, then restarted the server, and made it worse. Ishita, the senior, sat beside me and said, "Stop. What did it do first?" She wrote on paper: ran, ran again, stopped. One change, then look. It took forty minutes and I hated every one. It taught me to write before I touch.

qa.q: What did the report job do to every customer?
qa.a: The report job emailed itself twice to every customer.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling with the team standing behind the chair?
qa.a: Minakshi felt frightened and tunnel-visioned, with cold hands and a head that felt narrow, and rushed several changes.

qa.q: What choice did Ishita make that changed the situation?
qa.a: Ishita told Minakshi to stop and wrote down what the job did in order, which slowed things to one change and a look.

qa.q: How might Ishita have seen Minakshi's rushed changes?
qa.a: Ishita probably saw a frightened junior making things worse, and calmly used a written list instead of adding more guesses.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a first live failure with a racing heart, several rushed changes and a written one-change method.
